In the 1990s, Japan’s bullet trains had a *problem*.
Every time one burst out of a tunnel,
it fired a *boom*, like a cannon.
Air, squeezed ahead of the nose, *exploding* out of the exit.
People living nearby *complained*.
The engineer in charge, Eiji Nakatsu, was also a *birdwatcher*.
And he knew a bird that solves this exact problem *every day*.
The *kingfisher*.
It dives from air into water, two very different worlds,
and barely makes a *splash*.
The secret is its beak: *long*, *narrow*, almost *round*.
It parts the water instead of *slamming* into it.
So the team tested nose after nose,
and the closer it looked like a *kingfisher’s beak*, the better it ran.
The result: the *500 Series* Shinkansen.
A *15-metre* nose.
*30%* less air pressure.
*15%* less electricity,
while running *10%* faster.
Nature had already solved it.
We just had to *look*.
